title: Met to re-examine CCTV footage from unsolved Jill Dando murder
description: The TV presenter and newsreader was born in Weston-Super-Mare, Somerset, and worked for the BBC for 14 years. She was 37 when she died on the doorstep
body: The TV presenter and newsreader was born in Weston-Super-Mare, Somerset, and worked for the BBC for 14 years. She was 37 when she died on the doorstep of her home on Gowan Avenue.Soon after her death, a man of Serbian descent called the BBC claiming she had been executed in a revenge hit for the UK-backed Nato bombing of Serbia's state broadcaster in Belgrade.However, Barry George, a local man, was convicted of her murder and spent eight years in jail before being acquitted at a retrial in 2008. Dando's partner, Alan Farthing, was interviewed by the police, along with her ex-partner and BBC Breakfast news editor Bob Wheaton. Also interviewed was her agent Jon Roseman, who had written a crime novel detailing a very similar scene.They were all ruled out as suspects. Her killing was the subject of a Netflix documentary Who Killed Jill Dando? in 2023.Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to hello.bbclondon@bbc.co.uk, external

schema.headline: Met to re-examine CCTV footage from unsolved Jill Dando murder

title: Prince Harry says it is 'great' to be back in UK after six years in US
description: Meghan has largely stayed out of the public eye, with few public appearances.Harry has carried out several public engagements linked to his work with
body: Meghan has largely stayed out of the public eye, with few public appearances.Harry has carried out several public engagements linked to his work with the Invictus Games.Last week, he visited a school in Birmingham to launch an education programme inspired by the games, where he played pickleball with pupils and took part in a science lesson on prosthetic design.The games will take place in Birmingham from 10 to 17 July next year, with 550 wounded, injured and sick service personnel and veterans from 25 nations expected to compete in 12 adaptive sports.Harry spoke to CTV after completing a skydive in Toronto to honour a promise to a 102-year-old World War Two veteran and raise awareness of military charities.Asked what had prompted the family's return to the UK, Harry said there were "lots of reasons" but did not elaborate.The couple were reportedly surprised by a letter authorised by the King which reiterated that they are private citizens and set out guidance to senior government and military figures on how they should be treated.Prince Harry and King Charles have had a strained relationship since the Duke and Duchess of Sussex stepped down as senior working royals and moved to the US.Meanwhile, the Sussexes are waiting to hear whether they will receive taxpayer-funded security in the UK.The committee which oversees royal and VIP security, Ravec, is set to reconsider the family's level of police protection now that they are full-time residents rather than visitors.

schema.headline: Prince Harry says it is 'great' to be back in UK after six years in US

title: Athens explosion: Six dead in blast near Acropolis in Plaka district
description: Six people have died, including a British national, in an explosion that destroyed a building containing a holiday rental property in the historic cen
body: Six people have died, including a British national, in an explosion that destroyed a building containing a holiday rental property in the historic centre of Athens.The blast on Friday happened in the Plaka area of the Greek capital, a neighbourhood close to tourist sites such as the Acropolis.Four American holidaymakers were among the dead, along with a UK national and Greek national - reportedly an elderly couple who lived in the same building. Pictures from the scene on Saturday showed emergency service workers searching through rubble, with a gas leak the suspected cause of the blast.All six bodies had been recovered by Saturday afternoon. Athens Mayor Haris Doukas said: "We are talking about an incredible disaster."The tourists were confirmed to be missing when they did not arrive for their flight at Athens airport later on Friday, news agency Reuters reported citing local police.The three-storey building completely collapsed due to the force of the blast, with neighbouring buildings damaged and debris scattered across the road.

schema.headline: Athens explosion: Six dead in blast near Acropolis in Plaka district

title: Trump rejects Iran deal to reopen Strait of Hormuz in seven days
description: US President Donald Trump has rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz to commercial shipping within a week.He told reporters at th
body: US President Donald Trump has rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz to commercial shipping within a week.He told reporters at the White House that Tehran "want to make a deal where they open the Strait immediately because they're losing so badly".On Friday, Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told reporters at the UN in New York that agreement could be reached "if the necessary conditions are met" and that these were contained in a memorandum of understanding (MOU) signed by the two countries in June.The vital waterway through which around a fifth of the world's gas and oil supply usually flows has been effectively closed since the outbreak of war in February."I'm rejecting their deal," Trump said on Saturday, adding that the US already had "total control" of the strait, with "massive amounts of oil" passing through it. "They want to make a deal, and I think that's fine. I like making a deal, too. But that deal would not be acceptable," he added.On Friday the Wall Street Journal, external cited officials as saying Trump was sceptical that Iran would meet his demands and had told his staff that he saw a renewed bombing campaign as probable.Iran responded to US and Israeli air strikes, beginning in late February, by attacking Israel and US bases in the Gulf and Arab Gulf allies of the US - as well as blocking the Strait of Hormuz. Its closure has caused wild fluctuations of energy prices.The economic effects have also increased pressure on Trump to find a way of ending the conflict - particularly as the US heads towards Congressional elections in November.The MOU was designed to bring about a ceasefire and at least partly reopen the Strait of Hormuz. The 14-point agreement said Iran would never have a nuclear weapon. It noted that the US, Iran and their allies would end military operations on "all fronts" and contained provisions including ending a US naval blockade and other sanctions. But the deal fell apart after both sides resumed strikes. Iran has attacked vessels it says have attempted to cross the strait without authorisation.The US has attacked Iranian sites in the strait - as well as Iranian tankers off the country's coast. It has also maintained a blockade of Iranian ports, causing huge disruption to the Iranian economy.Trump has since claimed the US has been successful in getting oil out through the Strait of Hormuz. Shipping data shows a recent 10-day average of about 18 transits per day, with numbers dropping as low as nine vessels on certain days, according to Kpler, a commodities analytics firm cited by Reuters.The situation has been exacerbated by Houthi attacks on Saudi oil installations.Yemen's Houthis - allied to Iran - have recently intensified attacks aimed at disrupting Saudi oil exports via the Red Sea, on the other side of the Arabian peninsula to the Strait of Hormuz.The group seized strategic stretches of Yemen's Red Sea coast this month, including the port of Mokha, which overlooks the Bab al-Mandab Strait, another chokepoint for global shipping.

schema.headline: Trump rejects Iran deal to reopen Strait of Hormuz in seven days

title: Security lapses at Utah campus where Charlie Kirk was killed, review says
description: An independent review has pointed to a number of security shortcomings at the Utah campus where conservative activist Charlie Kirk was shot dead last
body: An independent review has pointed to a number of security shortcomings at the Utah campus where conservative activist Charlie Kirk was shot dead last year.The report said Utah Valley University (UVU) did not carry out a proper written security assessment nor prepare an event action plan, deferring key decision-making about the event to Kirk's conservative organisation Turning Point USA.It also said that Kirk's aides had insisted on a outdoor venue, overriding security concerns from campus officials, who then failed to properly assess the dangers.The 31-year-old activist had been addressing thousands of people in an Orem campus courtyard when he was shot from a nearby rooftop on 10 September 2025.Kirk's family said the report reinforced their concerns about how the event was managed.University officials had raised concerns in August 2025 about holding the event at a location surrounded by tall buildings and had suggested alternative venues, including some indoors, the report, external - published by UVU - says. "But a Turning Point representative insisted that Kirk speak at a campus courtyard because he had been there previously and the organisation was familiar with the location," it adds. Despite the "significant protective operations considerations", no line-of-sight assessment was documented in the planning process, the external consultants note.They also identified shortcomings in the co-ordination between university police and Kirk's private security team. A proposed meeting between the university's police chief and Turning Point security shortly before the event did not take place, the report said. The reviewers described the absence of a joint security briefing and walk-through as a missed opportunity to have identified risks, clarified responsibilities and considered additional security measures. However, the review concluded that no university employee or representative had acted in bad faith or shown "willful and wanton disregard" for anyone's safety.Kirk's family has previously accused the university of serious security failures and has filed a wrongful-death notice, a step that can precede legal action.The family's lawyer, Brett Parkinson, said the independent report released on Friday backed up the concerns raised by Kirk's loved ones."The buck stopped with UVU leadership and law enforcement," Parkinson said in a statement to the Associated Press. "Justice for Charlie and his family requires true accountability for UVU's fatal shortcomings that day."When asked for comment on the findings, Turning Point USA referred to Parkinson's statement.The review makes numerous recommendations aimed at improving security for major campus events. UVU President Jon Anderson said the university must "learn from the findings of this review, and follow through on its recommendations".It has previously been reported that the campus police failed to conduct security procedures that are common practice at US high-profile events, including flying a drone to monitor rooftops or security screening like bag checks and metal detectors.Kirk had been debating UVU students about US mass shootings, as part of a series of events across different university campuses, when he was shot in the neck shortly after noon. He was rushed to hospital but later pronounced dead.His alleged killer, Tyler Robinson, has pleaded not guilty to aggravated murder in connection with Kirk's death. Prosecutors are seeking the death penalty.

schema.headline: Security lapses at Utah campus where Charlie Kirk was killed, review says

title: Angela Rayner criticises worker visa plans on eve of Labour conference
description: Housing Secretary Angela Rayner has said she is concerned about Labour's proposals to change visa rules, which would make it harder for foreign worker
body: Housing Secretary Angela Rayner has said she is concerned about Labour's proposals to change visa rules, which would make it harder for foreign workers to secure permanent residency in the UK.In an interview with the Times, external ahead of Labour's annual conference, Rayner questioned Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood's plans, saying they are unfair because they "change the goalposts".Under the proposals, most migrants would have to wait 10 years to qualify for residency - instead of the current five - while foreign workers on health and social care visas would face a 15-year wait.Mahmood said the government would make a decision on the immigration overhaul by the end of the year.Speaking to the Times, Rayner said she was concerned about shifting "the goalposts years down the line" for people who arrived in the UK at the beginning of this decade, expecting to secure permanent residence under the current rules. She described the potential rule change as "very disruptive" and added: "I do have concerns about that." During her interview with the Times, she said that the changes would impact foreign care workers who "moved their lives here to look after our loved ones". Her remarks represent direct criticism of a policy inherited by Prime Minister Andy Burnham from his predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer.Rayner previously served as deputy prime minister under Sir Keir, and was brought back into cabinet by Burnham in July.It is significant that a serving cabinet minister feels able to criticise an existing government proposal on the eve of Labour's conference, albeit one inherited from the Starmer era.It is part of a growing head of steam from some parts of the party to quash the retrospective elements of these plans.Rayner has previously criticised the measures. In June, she said proposals to retrospectively alter the rules for migrants already working in the UK would be "wrong". Rayner said she believed that Mahmood was aware of her position, telling the Times she has "not changed [her] view" since re-entering the cabinet.Before he became prime minister, Burnham said he "understood" where Rayner was coming from on her criticisms of the migrant visa changes, telling reporters in June that Labour "would do well to listen to what Angela has to say".Rayner's call for a change of approach has been echoed by York Central Labour MP Rachael Maskell, who also wants a rethink from the home secretary.She told the Today programme that "technically and morally" what is being proposed represented "the wrong set of values" and would affect "people who have come [to Britain] to serve faithfully and are then told that they have to wait another 10 years" to secure British citizenship.In recent weeks, trade unions have put pressure on the government to soften its proposals, and a letter to Mahmood jointly signed by dozens of Labour MPs at the start of the year described the plans as "un-British". Lisa Nandy, secretary of state for culture, media and sport, rejected the "un-British" description of the plans.She told BBC Radio 4's Today programme: "I don't think they are un-British because I don't think that we have ever had an automatic right to citizenship for most people who come to the UK from overseas."Nandy said the home secretary was trying to balance respect for people "regardless of who they or where they stand" with the need for "an immigration system that people have confidence in".Asked if Labour could change its mind on the proposals, she told Today: "We always reserve the right to change our minds but we also will reserve the right to stick to our plans if we think we are getting them right".The culture secretary said the government will not "change the rules of the game" in a way that unfairly disadvantages migrants who have contributed to the UK.She said it would "strike the right balance" between treating people "fairly and decently as human beings but making sure there is an asylum and immigration system people can have confidence in."Nandy's comments are a hint the government is reconsidering. She could have given a full-throated defence of the principle of backdating the changes so they apply to those foreign workers already here. But she did not. Instead she emphasised the principle of those "contributing" to the UK and treating them fairly.But if the government does reverse course on applying these changes to those arriving from 2021, the large numbers who came to the UK after that date have a quicker and easier route to settlement. That is a dividing line with the Conservatives and Reform UK that those parties will be keen to highlight.The home secretary faced questions about the changes during an appearance at the Home Affairs Committee earlier this month.Mahmood said she was "very aware that a large group of people who arrived in 2022, absent any change, would qualify in February 2027" for permanent settlement.She added: "Later this year we will set out the new policy on settlement... as well as any transitional arrangements we might decide to implement."

schema.headline: Angela Rayner criticises worker visa plans on eve of Labour conference

title: Israel v Republic of Ireland: Republic of Ireland to wear black armbands for Israel game
description: Republic of Ireland players intend to wear black armbands "in recognition of all lives lost in the [Gaza] conflict" for Sunday's Nations League game a
body: Republic of Ireland players intend to wear black armbands "in recognition of all lives lost in the [Gaza] conflict" for Sunday's Nations League game against Israel in Hungary, after confirming they will go ahead with the fixture.Football Association of Ireland (FAI) chief executive David Courell confirmed one player has withdrawn from the squad before the match.But he added that a vote among the squad produced a "significant majority" in favour of playing.As well as the intention to wear black armbands for Sunday's 'away' game against Israel in Debrecen, Courell said the players will make further gestures for the initial game and the return 'home' fixture against Israel next Sunday in Serbia.The fixtures have been embroiled in controversy since the two teams were drawn to play each other in Group B3.Republic of Ireland players faced calls to withdraw from the games because of the ongoing Israel-Gaza war with a "Stop The Game" campaign - organised by the pressure group Irish Sport for Palestine - gathering pace."One of their requests is to remove their media obligations for the remainder of this window," Courell said at Saturday's delayed news conference."They also have the intention to wear black armbands in recognition of all lives lost in the [Gaza] conflict. "There will be elements of the pre-match ceremony not be partaken in by the Republic of Ireland and it is also the intention of the players to make a significant contribution to charitable donation by virtue of both [Israel] match fees and also the fixture against Austria at the Aviva [Stadium in Dublin on Thursday]."There appeared to be real doubt on Saturday morning whether the fixture would take place.A pre-match news conference with manager Heimir Hallgrimsson and a player, scheduled for 09:15 BST, was postponed just 15 minutes before it was scheduled to start, with reporters informed it would instead take place after the team's training session which was also delayed.The players were locked in a meeting back at their hotel after it emerged a player, goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu, withdrew from the game in protest with several other expressing their concerns about fielding.Around 13:00 BST, players began to filter out of the meeting room, with it then confirmed the news conference would indeed go ahead, back at Nagyerdei Stadion at 14:30, with training to follow.More than five hours after the initial news conference was scheduled to begin, Courell - flanked by Hallgrimsson and FAI director of football John Martin - confirmed a players' vote passed by a "significant majority" to play the game."This morning, a player expressed their discomfort at the fixture and indicated their intent to withdraw," Courell said."This new variable required time for the rest of the squad to consider and what proceeded was another four hours of conversations, predominantly among the players, but also at times with coaching staff and the [FAI] executive."There were a lot of positions presented and the association is fully respectful of everyone's right to their respective opinion."Former Republic of Ireland manager Brian Kerr and ex-international James McClean are among those to have backed calls for a boycott of the fixtures.The armed Palestinian group Hamas attacked Israel on 7 October 2023, killing about 1,200 people and taking 251 hostages.In response, Israel launched a massive military offensive in Gaza, during which more than 73,000 people have been killed, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations.Hallgrimsson relayed that nobody "can understand the pressure that has been going on these players" and said the lengthy meeting on Saturday stemmed from "a change of mind for one of the players to play the game"."All of the rest of the players are training today," he confirmed."The balance [to play] changed with this [withdrawal] and obviously it was an ongoing discussion but we came to a conclusion and the game is going ahead."We will train and there will probably be more discussions tonight and probably tomorrow. It's a unique situation and we are just trying to limit the damage."The Republic of Ireland lost their opening Nations League fixture in Kosovo on Thursday, a match overshadowed in the build-up by the Israel games.Asked whether the far from ideal preparation for Sunday's game would affect the players, the Irish boss said "we will see"."Nobody is comfortable but it's about limiting the damage, both personally and for Irish football, that we need to find some solution on it," Hallgrimsson added."There is no action we do that everyone will agree to, so we need to find a solution to limit the damage for us as a group, for Ireland as a nation and the association for football in Ireland."We don't know the consequences if we don't play the game but a lot of players share a common feeling, so there are two choices and both are tough. It's a situation you can't win."A spokesperson for the Irish governement insists any decision regarding the fixtures lie firmly at the door of the FAI and Uefa."The FAI had decided to play the fixtures against Israel in accordance with their obligations as members of Uefa. Following engagement with players today decision stands," they said."The FAI has strongly represented the views of its membership that Israel should be excluded from international football competitions, including bringing a motion to Uefa to this effect last year. The reality is that this motion was not passed by Uefa and that the FAI was obliged to fulfil the fixture."Israel Football Association [IFA] head of communications Shlomi Barzel commended the Republic of Ireland team for confirming they will play, saying "football has won".Barzel began Israel's news conference with a statement before requesting  questions regarding the game-only were directed towards captain Dor Peretz and head coach Ran Ben-Shimon who remained on script."The separation between football and politics must be maintained, any other approach spell chaos," he said, confirming Israel players intend to shake hands before the game."The Irish football association [FAI] and the national team players did he right thing by recognising this, even if it took a bit longer than it should. Yet, it is better to be late than never."The one who certainly lost today are those who want to intimidate to separate and turn the football pitch into a political arena. Uefa, the IFA [Israel Football and the FAI stood strong together to prevent it."Barzel also confirmed the IFA intend to appeal both yellow cards shown to Sayed Abu Farhi in Thursday's 3-1 defeat by Austria.Abu Farhi was shown a second yellow for his goal celebration which Barzel insists was not mimicking the firing of a gun, but an "imitation of a snooker player, like the legendary Ken Doherty."

schema.headline: Israel v Republic of Ireland: Republic of Ireland to wear black armbands for Israel game

title: Murder or medical mix-up? New questions in the Colin Norris case
description: The podcast series comes a week after a public inquiry reported on the case of former neonatal nurse Lucy Letby who was convicted of murdering seven b
body: The podcast series comes a week after a public inquiry reported on the case of former neonatal nurse Lucy Letby who was convicted of murdering seven babies and attempting to murder seven others at a hospital in Chester a decade ago. While the circumstances are very different, Norris' supporters also argue that his case hinges on disputed interpretations of medical evidence.The story begins in 2002 when Norris, a 26-year-old nurse, originally from Glasgow, found Ethel in an hypoglycemic coma as she recovered from a broken hip.Doctors took blood samples to find out what caused her blood sugar to drop so low. The test results seemed conclusive - she had a massive amount of insulin in her blood. She died 21 days later, sparking a murder investigation.A nurse who had been on shift on the night Ethel was found told the police that Norris had predicted the 86-year-old might not last the night. He quickly became the prime suspect.The police operation trawled retrospectively through all the deaths on Norris's wards, looking for potential murders that may have gone unnoticed.They identified three other cases of unexplained severe hypoglycemic deaths and one where the patient recovered.No blood tests had been taken from these cases at the time of their deaths to be able to prove insulin poisoning but experts for the prosecution said in court that their medical charts showed persistent and severe low blood sugar readings.They said that because this was so rare in non-diabetics that it must be murder.When it came to court in 2007, experts called by the defence said four of the five patients had died of natural causes.But after a five-month trial and a deadlocked jury, Norris was convicted by a majority of 11-1 and told he would not be eligible for parole for 30 years.After the verdict, Ethel's son Stuart Hall said: "I don't think he should come out again. He's got the knowledge to commit murder but do it discreetly."When I got involved in the case in 2009, Norris, who is now known as Colin Campbell, had just lost his first appeal against conviction.Two years later, new scientific evidence came to light which challenged one of the key assumptions underpinning the prosecution case. It claimed hypoglycemia - low blood sugar - in the frail and elderly is not as vanishingly rare as was once thought, suggesting the jury had been misinformed.This new evidence was submitted for a second appeal, which took another 14 years to be heard.During that appeal last year, experts for Norris argued that the symptoms seen in several of the patients could occur naturally in elderly, frail people.Experts for the Crown maintained the deaths were medically distinct.They said their blood sugar readings were refractory, meaning they kept coming back despite being given glucose, whereas naturally-occurring hypoglycemia can be easily corrected with a treatment such as a sugary drink.They argued this distinction could only be explained by deliberate insulin poisoning.Were the syringes accidentally switched?Initially, we discounted this scenario because we assumed medical staff would be alerted if a diabetic patient had accidentally been given dextrose instead of insulin.  However, endocrinologist Prof Joel Zonszein, an expert in diabetes, said the amount given would not have caused a severe illness."The answer is very different from somebody getting insulin," he said. "Insulin is much more aggressive. Giving too much sugar does not cause a coma and it will take more that 24 hours until the person goes into a coma. It's completely different."Prof Zonszein also said the amount of insulin Ethel may have been given accidentally would have produced the high readings in her immunoassay blood test taken five hours later.He said the drip of dextrose would have masked the insulin, making it harder to notice, but the blood test result would still register a very high level of insulin.If the syringes were accidentally switched, is that a mix-up rather than a murder?That still leaves another question: what caused Ethel to fall into a coma in the first place?Our investigation found all five patients had been prescribed medications, all were on antibiotics and two of the women were on powerful painkillers.All of these are known to increase the risk of severe hypoglycaemia in frail, elderly patients.It is possible that a strong opioid prescribed to Ethel for her post-op pain put her in a coma, and insulin meant for somebody else was accidentally given to her before the blood sample, which proved poisoning, was taken.The Court of Appeal ruled last year on whether naturally-occurring hypoglycaemia could explain the medical collapse of the four patients beyond Ethel Hall but ruled the case put by Norris' team got nowhere close to undermining the safety of his convictions and rejected the appeal on all grounds.They also rejected Norris' lawyers' attempts to go to the Supreme Court. An application has been made to the European Court of Human Rights, by Norris' lawyers, but solicitor Rory Hearty says this "hurdle" will take many years.

schema.headline: Murder or medical mix-up? New questions in the Colin Norris case

title: Keep dancing: 100-year-old leads Worcester charity flash mob
description: A 100-year-old man, already known for his dance moves through social media, led a flash mob with hundreds of people joining in.Wearing a bright red sh
body: A 100-year-old man, already known for his dance moves through social media, led a flash mob with hundreds of people joining in.Wearing a bright red shirt, Bernard Gilbert directed a dance to song King of the Road by country singer Roger Miller in Worcester city centre, with crowds erupting in applause after he finished.The former dance teacher previously went viral on social media for his moves at Fernhill House Care Home where he lives. His videos were seen more than 1.5m times."I love the dancing, once I get on the floor I forget everything, I just concentrate on what I'm doing," he said when the BBC interviewed him in June. The flash mob in Cathedral Square featured Got2Sing choir members as well as residents as they raised money for Alzheimer's Research UK. They learnt four dances, practised hard and rehearsed at home to prepare for the event, Fernhill House Care Home said."What an inspiring day, what a community, what a fantastic memory we've created together," it added.Organisers of Got2Sing Worcester described the flash mob as a "joyful afternoon" with singers "bringing their energy and talent" to the city centre."When a 100-year-old local legend leads the line dancing, you know it's going to be a good afternoon," they said.

schema.headline: Keep dancing: 100-year-old leads Worcester charity flash mob

title: England 26-19 New Zealand: Red Roses return to winning ways in WXV Global Series
description: England's Harrison scores last-gasp try to beat Black FernsFigure caption, England secure win over New Zealand with last-gasp tryByAlastair TelferBBC
body: England's Harrison scores last-gasp try to beat Black FernsFigure caption, England secure win over New Zealand with last-gasp tryByAlastair TelferBBC Sport journalist at Allianz StadiumWXV Global SeriesEngland (7) 26Tries: Moloney-MacDonald, Kildunne, Breach, Harrison Cons: Harrison 3New Zealand (12) 19Tries: Du Plessis, Leti-I'iga, Paul Cons: Sorensen-McGee 2Zoe Harrison scored a last-gasp try as England defeated New Zealand at Allianz Stadium to avoid a second successive draw in the WXV Global Series.With the scores level at 19-19 in the 81st minute and having missed a penalty moments earlier, Harrison intercepted a pass as the Black Ferns tried to counter-attack, the fly-half diving over the line and piled up on by celebrating team-mates. The world champions' record 39-game winning run came to an end last weekend in the 26-26 draw with Canada, but this week they were able to find a dramatic path to victory, much to the delight of the 59,871 crowd.New Zealand, the last team to beat England in the World Cup final in 2022, suffered their first defeat under new head coach Whitney Hansen.The Black Ferns had taken a deserved lead at half-time after tries from Amy du Plessis and Ayesha Leti-I'iga ruled out Claudia Moloney-MacDonald's opening score.Tries by Ellie Kildunne and Jess Breach restored John Mitchell's side's lead, before Mererangi Paul's converted try drew the game level on 70 minutes.England now travel to Canada to complete their three-Test series against the World Cup finalists in Toronto and Ottawa, while the Black Ferns play France in Hamilton.Figure caption, 'Absolutely brilliant' - Moloney-MacDonald try puts Red Roses in frontRugby's great rivalry comes alive againThe Black Ferns have beaten the Red Roses in all five World Cup final meetings they have contested.Canada outclassed New Zealand in last year's World Cup semi-final to deny a repeat of what is one of rugby's great rivalries.Under Hansen, who took over as head coach after last year's disappointing World Cup, the Black Ferns were unbeaten and have defeated Canada and France this year.The world's second-ranked side spent a large chunk of the first half deep in England's 22, and an opportunistic kick found unmarked space for Du Plessis to dot down for a deserved try.England comfortably beat New Zealand 49-31 in their most recent meeting in 2024, winning all three encounters since their 2022 World Cup final defeat, which has opened the door for Canada to become the Red Roses' toughest contest.However, the years were rolled back in Twickenham as Hansen's side brought a fearsome level of physicality and speed to challenge the Red Roses.Leti-I'iga, who had an opening try ruled out, caused havoc throughout the first half and finally crossed after Tyla King broke clear, before a poorly judged cross-field kick, with another try beckoning, let Mitchell's side off the hook.Figure caption, King splits defence with 'brilliant dummy' to set up Leti-I'iga tryEngland learn lessons to close out winEngland have not led at half-time in any of their Global WXV Series games.Given their season only began two weeks ago against Australia, Mitchell has been quick to defend his side's rustiness.Individual magic from Kildunne, who spotted a gap on the wing for her try, and a yellow card for a high shot by Veisinia Mahutariki-Fakalelu, presented Mitchell with an opportunity to empty his bench with momentum behind his side.Breach's simple finish came in the next play as any fears of a first loss in four years began to dissolve.But the Black Ferns refused to go away and continued to trouble England's defence, which is now being influenced by coaching consultant Shaun Edwards.Mitchell's side were criticised for turning down a kickable penalty late in the game against Canada.The opportunity again presented itself, and Harrison took it on from distance, but the ball came up well short.Canada opted to kick the ball out and accept the draw last week, which is not in the DNA of New Zealand, and they attacked from distance in an attempt to inflict England's first loss on home soil since 2016.That proved to be the wrong decision, as a pass was picked off deep inside the visitors' 22, and instead the Red Roses won their 14th straight game at Allianz Stadium.Figure caption, Late Harrison try seals dramatic win for England over New ZealandEngland: Kildunne; Breach, Jones (capt), Rowland, Moloney-MacDonald; Harrison, L Packer; Carson, Field, Bern, Talling, Ives Campion, Matthews, Kabeya, FeaunatiReplacements: Campbell, Botterman, Muir, Burton, Packer, Hunt, Heard, SingNew Zealand: Sorensen-McGee; Paul, Brunt, Du Plessis, Leti-I'iga; H King, Joseph; Viliko, Ponsonby, Mahutariki-Fakalelu, Roos, Bayfield, Mikaele-Tu'u, E-P King, Olsen-BakerReplacements: Lolohea, Robinson, Taumata, Vaipulu, Sae, Turner, McGregor, SailiOfficialsReferee: Clara Munarini (Italy)Assisant referees: Ben Connor (Wales) and Beatrice Smussi (Italy)TMO: Quinton Immelman (South Africa)

schema.headline: England 26-19 New Zealand: Red Roses return to winning ways in WXV Global Series

title: Manchester City charges: Khaldoon Al Mubarak confident club will prove innocence
description: Figure caption, Kieran Maguire on potential sanctions for Man CityByPaul BattisonBBC Sport Journalist and Ffion WynneBBC Sport JournalistUpdated 3 hou
body: Figure caption, Kieran Maguire on potential sanctions for Man CityByPaul BattisonBBC Sport Journalist and Ffion WynneBBC Sport JournalistUpdated 3 hours agoManchester City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak says he is still confident of proving the club's innocence after they were found guilty of breaking the Premier League's financial rules.City were accused of a wide range of rule breaches, centring around claims they inflated sponsorship revenue from connected companies and made other "off the books" payments to circumvent financial regulations.On Friday, it was announced City had been found guilty of the vast majority of the 115 charges brought against them and Al Mubarak has responded with a letter to fans on the club's website. "Following Friday's media reporting, many of you will have spent your evening answering questions and responding to messages from friends, family and colleagues. So have I," Al Mubarak said."Here's what I said to my family: The Premier League process still has a long way to run, and our confidence and intent in proving the club's innocence is just as strong as when this began."There are so many things that I would like to be able to share with you to help you understand why we feel so confident in our position. "But the strict confidentiality of the legal process and our determination to respect it means I cannot do that at the moment. Even this letter underwent several legal checks to make sure it complies."Premier League clubs are seeking legal advice about compensation relating to the charges, while BBC Sport has been told City will appeal.Sanctions on the club are yet to be announced, but repercussions could include a points deduction, expulsion from the Premier League or a huge fine. Al Mubarak, who was appointed as City's chairman after their 2008 takeover, also said his club was being "undermined". "While some people have been quick to reach their own conclusions, and there is so much noise swirling around us, nothing has changed. We have faced challenges together before and have prevailed," he added."There remain many who want to undermine the momentum of our club. We will not give them that opportunity."Meanwhile, Christian Purslow, a former Liverpool managing director and Aston Villa chief executive, who also held a senior role at Chelsea, said the City case could begin a chain of events that would be "appalling for the game".Speaking on Radio 4's Today programme, Purslow appeared alongside football law expert Paul Gilroy KC, who described the case as a "seismic moment for world football".Purslow said: "It's a sort of 'where does this end?' because if you look at every single season - the nine seasons which we now know Manchester City breached rules - then all of their 19 Premier League rivals in that season, to differing extents, suffered easy-to-compute loss. Whether it was a place in the Premier League - every place was worth £3m."Teams that came fifth who didn't make the Champions League maybe lost tens of millions of pounds - and of course teams that were relegated. Let's say the team that finished 18th would've finished 17th if Manchester City weren't there. And they, of course, suffered huge loss."If you add all those claims up, over nine years, and that's just in the Premier League, you can see that the potential here for this to spiral out of control is huge."Gilroy added that, so far, four clubs have put in protective claims "reserving the right to claim compensation if City are found guilty".'Very unsettling for football fans'The news, broken by the Athletic,, external came 1,327 days after City were charged by the Premier League in February 2023 following a four-year investigation, and 22 months after a hearing by an independent commission concluded.No official announcement has been made by the Premier League, which has declined to comment.Manchester City declined to comment on whether they had been found guilty, instead providing a statement which read: "Premier League process remains ongoing with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality."The club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League board and executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence."Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy has urged the Premier League to come to a quick resolution.She told BBC Radio 5 Live: "I think most football fans will be feeling that this is not a good moment for football as a whole and I think Manchester City fans will be feeling very, very anxious about what happens next."It's very unsettling for football fans and I hope that it can be resolved as swiftly as possible."I will obviously look very closely as what comes out of this but we can't apply those rules for the Premier League. They have got to do it themselves and are going to have to resolve this as swiftly as possible - not just for the sake of Manchester City but for the sake of football."Figure caption, What do Man City charges mean and what happens next?Former chairman Bernstein feels 'absolutely awful'City won eight trophies in the period covered by the case, including three Premier League titles, three EFL Cups, one Community Shield and one FA Cup.The charges cover the managerial tenures of Roberto Mancini and Manuel Pellegrini, and the first two years under Pep Guardiola, who left the club at the end of last season after 10 years in charge.David Bernstein, who was Manchester City chairman from 1998-2003, told Times Radio he felt "absolutely awful" on hearing the news of City being found guilty - but admitted any punishment would have to be "more drastic" than a fine. "To see all this tarnished in this way is very sad," he said."I feel particularly bad for the wonderful supporters of the club who've stayed with the club through thick and thin."This whole process has taken too long already. So the appeal process now has to be done quickly because you've got the club playing with this cloud over its head and it's just not viable."The appeal process cannot go on for year after year, I think that would be a disaster, not just for this particular case but for English football generally. The timing is crucial."He continued: "I can't give a view on the punishment. If they are found, after the appeal, guilty of 115 charges, my beloved club is going to face a very severe penalty."All I would say is that money is not sufficient, it would have to be something, unfortunately, more drastic than that."Meanwhile, singer-songwriter Noel Gallagher says he is "shocked" at the news and it is "quite sad" for players and fans."A little surprised when I heard it on the radio. Surprised because the club have assured us all along that they vehemently denied any of these charges," the Oasis star and City fan said on the Let Me Talk podcast."So it was a bit of a shock to find out that we've been found guilty. But really overall just quite sad really. Sad for the fans and for the players."Follow Manchester City on BBC SoundsPre-match, post-match and topical City contentSubscribe and listen for everything you love about City

schema.headline: Manchester City charges: Khaldoon Al Mubarak confident club will prove innocence

title: Heathrow Airport warns third runway could be delayed by four years
description: Heathrow Airport has warned that its planned third runway might be delayed by four years due to planning and regulatory issues.The government had hope
body: Heathrow Airport has warned that its planned third runway might be delayed by four years due to planning and regulatory issues.The government had hoped the new runway at the UK's busiest airport, estimated to cost £33bn, would open by 2035.But Heathrow sees this deadline as increasingly difficult to deliver without further steps to simplify the planning process. It said on Saturday that it hoped to secure planning permission by 2029 and then open the runway "within a decade".The Department for Transport (DfT) said the project's timeline had "always been ambitious" and that it would continue to work with stakeholders "at pace" on the matter.The airport said its "core scenario" had always been to open a new runway within a decade of securing planning permission.It said it was encouraged by the chancellor's efforts to streamline infrastructure and remove regulatory bottlenecks, and promised to continue to work with ministers, airlines and stakeholders to "progress the planning application with pace".Former chancellor Rachel Reeves announced the government's support for the project in January 2025 as a means to grow the economy, and Prime Minister Andy Burnham - who was previously critical - said he was "open-minded" about the scheme when he came to office.Despite attracting wide opposition from environmental campaigners and local resident groups, the project is expected to create around 100,000 jobs and provide a major boost to the economy as part of a wider £49bn modernisation of the airport.The expansion would mean demolishing hundreds of homes, diverting rivers, and rerouting the M25 motorway between junctions 14 and 15 through a tunnel under the new runway.The number of flights from the site, currently capped at 480,000 a year, could go up to 720,000 - or nearly 2,000 a day on average.A DfT spokesperson said: "There is currently no live planning application for a third runway, and we cannot comment on ongoing consultation processes or prejudice them in a way that will only delay progress."The timeline has always been ambitious. We'll continue to work with promoters, including Heathrow, and all other stakeholders at pace to ensure the right framework is in place for which a planning application for a third runway could be considered."A spokesperson for Heathrow said: "It's right that ambitious targets were set; the sooner expansion begins, the sooner the whole UK will benefit."They said the benefits would involve "at least 108,000 new jobs and billions of pounds invested in supply chains in every part of the country"."This is a national project, 100% privately financed which will support growth today and secure the UK's position in the global economy once the runway opens."Heathrow is the UK's busiest airport, serving more than 80 million travellers a year with its four passenger terminals and two runways.Correction 26 September: An earlier version of this story said the runway was estimated to cost £49bn. It has been updated to reflect that this figure is the total amount of investment planned for the airport, including £33bn for the runway.

schema.headline: Heathrow Airport warns third runway could be delayed by four years

title: Azerbaijan Grand Prix: George Russell 'comes through other side' after 'real tough period'
description: Image source, ReutersImage caption, George Russell's victory in Azerbaijan was his third of the 2026 seasonByF1 CorrespondentFor George Russell, this
body: Image source, ReutersImage caption, George Russell's victory in Azerbaijan was his third of the 2026 seasonByF1 CorrespondentFor George Russell, this one felt like vindication, proof that he had "come through the other side" and was back to his best after what he acknowledged was a "real tough period" during this Formula 1 season.The Mercedes driver's victory in the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, holding off Red Bull's Max Verstappen in one of the closest finishes in history, was his first since the end of June - seven races ago.In that time, team-mate Kimi Antonelli has won three times, to take his tally of victories to eight for the season.So Russell needed this, his third victory, in a year that he started as championship favourite. Instead, Antonelli has taken the season by the throat and all but crushed the life out of Russell's hopes.Now, though, a glimmer of hope still exists for Russell, even if he is too realistic to think too much about it for now.His win, combined with Antonelli's fifth place after what the Italian admitted was his "worst weekend of the year in terms of performance", has cut the points gap between them to 66.That's still huge, with either seven or eight races still to go, and 25 points for a win. But it's a lot better than the 81-point margin Russell faced before Baku."My team-mate's had an incredible season," Russell said. "He's been pretty flawless throughout, but now we're getting to crunch time."But I'm just going to focus on myself. You know, if I continue delivering performances like I've done this weekend, no matter what happens towards the end of the season, I'll be happy."With the grand prix brought forward 24 hours from the usual Sunday slot, it was an appropriate result for a man whose prowess in qualifying has earned him the nickname 'Mr Saturday'.Russell has been through the mill in 2026. He dominated the intra-team battle last year, but the tables have turned dramatically this season, as Antonelli felt immediately at home in the new Mercedes after the biggest rule changes in F1 history, and the Briton very much did not.For Russell, the blows have kept coming. Every apparent revival was met with another setback. Every time he felt he had made progress, Antonelli's apparently effortless way of extracting that little bit more from the car chastened him.No experience was more painful than the Italian Grand Prix at Monza two races ago, when Russell started from the front row, and Antonelli 19th after a grid penalty.Russell knew it was a golden opportunity to make up ground. Instead, it was Antonelli who won the race, with what will go down as one of the greatest drives in history. Russell looked on the verge of tears after that one.But he kept the belief, and in Baku it all came together.Antonelli 'wasn't really present'Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Kimi Antonelli finished off the podium for the first time since the British Grand PrixRussell was a man on a mission all weekend, fastest from the moment he took to the track, while Antonelli, after losing half the two hours of practice on the first day, lost his cool.He made a mistake in qualifying, took a wheel off on an inside wall, and started 16th. There was to be no repeat of Monza, even if fifth was a very creditable comeback result."I felt always a step behind," Antonelli said, "and especially with the mistake in qualifying the confidence level was not high and today was about damage limitation."Just probably also the mindset was not in the best place. I wasn't there. I wasn't really present, especially with what happened so early on and just didn't take the same risks, especially after qualifying."Today was more damage-safe mode instead of full attack. I just make sure next weekend we get back in the right level."If he does, this will go down as a blip in an otherwise stunningly impressive breakthrough season by a potential future great. But the parallels with last year are unavoidable.In 2025, McLaren's Oscar Piastri arrived in Azerbaijan apparently in control of the championship, and possessing a big lead over team-mate Lando Norris, albeit less than half what Antonelli's is now.But Piastri had some kind of meltdown on the streets of Baku, what he described after arriving back in the city this week as "the worst race of my career".And after that, the wheels came off for the Australian, and he was overtaken by the end of the year not only by Norris, but also by Verstappen.There is no reason to believe Antonelli will suffer the same fate. But he still has something to process in the few days before taking to the track again in Malaysia on Friday.'The most dominant weekend I've had in my career'Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Russell led from start to finish in AzerbaijanThis was the first time Russell has produced a weekend like this all year, when he was simply superior. Before, even when he won, Antonelli was right there with him, sometimes even faster.How did Russell do this? It has taken hard work and analysis on his part and with his engineers.He hasn't been comfortable in this year's car, feeling it does not suit his driving style, so he has had to put in the effort to make the driving feel natural. And he feels he is finally getting somewhere.Deputy team principal Bradley Lord said: "He had some difficult moments before the summer break, some soul-searching as well at points, and he's come back really strong, focused on the driving, focusing on the essentials of what he needs to do to put his weekends together step by step."Russell said: "I'm very proud of the resilience that I and my close group of engineers have shown during the tough periods this year because there's been a lot of hard work to overcome some of the challenges, to adapt my driving style to suit this new car better."And F1 is so tough, you don't get opportunities to practise this, and finally it's coming to me a bit more intuitively than it once did, and I'm gaining confidence. And especially on circuits like this, it just allows you to eke out that little bit more on the brakes, get that little bit closer to the walls, and it's been a flawless weekend."It's been four races since the (summer) break. I've been on the front row in three of them, three podiums from the four races. I feel I can fight for victory week in, week out now."The win was looking comfortable for a while, as he romped away at the front in the first stint while Piastri delayed Verstappen.But two mid-race safety cars closed up the field and left Verstappen right on Russell's tail.Russell could not shake him off, but he continued to be flawless. Even when slowing for a yellow flag on the final lap caused a loss of turbo boost pressure and left him vulnerable on the run to the flag."It's for sure the most dominant weekend I've had in my career," Russell said. "So that has come at a really great moment. And also to achieve it on a circuit that requires so much commitment and confidence, I'm really proud of, because it would have been very easy for me to lose the faith this season."Mercedes have lost their early season dominance over the summer, but the Bahrain/Malaysia race will see their first big upgrade for a while."I'm really excited," Russell said. "That's going to be a good step forward."Our car has been working exceptionally well on the low-drag circuits. We've got a really efficient car, so here at Baku we've been exceptionally fast. But I think from next week onwards, we're hoping to make a bigger step to the rest of the field. But nothing's sure until we see how it pans out in reality."And even if Antonelli cannot be anything but still a strong favourite, the same goes for the championship."There's much less pressure on me than there is on him," Russell said. "Yesterday was probably his first mistake of this whole season in a proper session, qualifying, race, and he still came home in P5 today."I didn't really consider myself in this fight for a number of races, purely because my performance wasn't strong enough."Now I feel like if the season were to have started today, or since the summer break, you know, I feel very much I would have been able to fight."Now I've got this big deficit. It can change quick. So I'm not chasing that. I'm chasing to win every race, and what will be, will be."

schema.headline: Azerbaijan Grand Prix: George Russell 'comes through other side' after 'real tough period'

title: Classy or classist? How bare nails became a hot issue
description: In recent months, Paloma Buddemeier has watched a stream of people walk into her nail salon with the goal of looking as if they'd never been there at
body: In recent months, Paloma Buddemeier has watched a stream of people walk into her nail salon with the goal of looking as if they'd never been there at all."It's crazy," the owner of Wumman Spa in London says.These customers still get their nails filed, buffed, and trimmed. "You still do the cuticle, you do the soaking and hydrate everything," says Buddemeier, "but you just put no polish on."Driving this, she says, is a viral craze for bare-looking nails.In recent months, artsy shots of glossy naked nails have been flooding social media and taking over fashion runways and red carpets, which some are viewing as the latest symbol of "quiet luxury".But critics argue the bare nails trend actually says something about class, the hamster wheel of beauty standards, and who gets to define what is considered tasteful.Nail art's historical and creative roots are linked back to black, Latino, and Asian communities and the suggestion that bare nails are now a sign of high status could stigmatise bold manicures, they say."That trend really promotes blankness and this kind of sameness and erasure of culture and identity that is so important to black and brown communities," beauty journalist Kristina Rodulfo tells the BBC."They are often called elegant or tasteful, and these are often usually euphemisms that perpetuate white supremacist standards of beauty."For some, though, the choice is less about a dislike of bold nails and more about simplifying their routine.Some converts say they're ditching polish as a way of rebelling against an entrenched female beauty standard or to save time and money. Others just love the look. Then, there are some women who've long left their nails alone, amused to find their routine – or lack thereof – suddenly in vogue.For years, Irish TV presenter Angela Scanlon marched herself to a nail salon every fortnight, a routine that started when she was living in New York in the 2000s. There, she says, manicures were so universal they felt like a uniform. But it soon became a chore.Scanlon would have everything from thin, shiny shellac to sturdier "Builder In A Bottle" gel manicures layered onto her nails every other week without fail."It wasn't like I was in my head going: 'I must go because Dave from Hull is going to be disgusted if I'm on This Morning next week without a full set'," the Radio 2 presenter says. "I just added it to the list of things that we must do... in the way you would wash your hair."Eventually, in a moment of clarity, Scanlon decided to stop going, in a bid to free up time and mental bandwidth."I heard myself saying to people: 'Ugh, my god, I have to go and get my nails done.'"And I thought: 'I probably don't need to do this anymore'."Scanlon's posts about her decision to ditch the continuous manicure blew up on Substack and Instagram earlier this year. She seemed to have tapped into a vein.Simple nails were in the spotlight at New York Fashion Week in February, with Marc Jacobs among those sending his models out polish-less, though some fashionistas argue this is not new.But beauty magazines have declared "All The Cool Girls Are Quietly Quitting Manicures, external", that "Bare Nails Are the New Status Symbol, external" of "Polished Women" and that "Manicures Are No Longer Classy, external".And there's a never-ending stream of posts on Insta and TikTok promoting shiny, natural-looking nails, and detailing how you can get them yourself. The look has become so hyped some have gone full circle, booking in salon appointments to mimic it.At the Wumman Spa nail salon, some of Buddemeier's clients sit in the chair for hours, as nail artists build them hyper-realistic fake nails in sheer, glossy neutrals, à la Zoe Kravitz and Zendaya.Londoner Khadija says she was once a fan of elaborate nail art but pivoted to bare nails earlier this year."It's just really chic. And I love less is more, I love minimalism... less consumerism and just self-care things that you could probably do at home."Reluctantly joining the bandwagon thanks to the rising cost of living is her friend Emmanuella. "It's just too expensive now," she says."I think getting [your] nails done is tacky now, because who's got an hour to waste?" one 25-year-old tells the BBC, adding, "also, I lift weights in the gym, so I don't want to snap a nail and waste money."But there are those who think the trend - or the way it's being discussed by some - belies something more sinister.Manicures have been whispering messages about the wearer's position in society for as long as they have existed, according to fashion journalist Suzanne E. Shapiro."Women's bodies - and sense of self-presentation - have always held huge political and cultural significance," Shapiro, who wrote Nails: The Story of The Modern Manicure, tells the BBC.Even back in 13th century Imperial China, the lengthy talons grown by nobility and the delicately carved brass nail shields which usually guarded them were a symbol of a life unmarred by manual labour.A single layer of the rose-tinted waxy salves which were popular in the 1800s was a sign of vigour and health, but two layers - in an era when cosmetics and artificial beauty were tied to virtue - was the mark of a vain or "loose" woman.And the red at-home nail lacquer, released by Revlon in the early 1930s, was a badge of honour for modern women rebelling against that kind of oppressive judgement.But it was women of colour who really made manicures an accessible and fashionable form of self-expression, historians say.Entertainer Josephine Baker, disco icons Diana Ross and Donna Summer, and Olympic gold-medal-winning sprinter Florence Griffith-Joyner - whose dramatic acrylic sets often distracted headline writers from her record-setting performances - have all pioneered nail art.And when waves of Vietnamese refugees gave rise to the nail bar in the 1970s, professional manicures were no longer the preserve of the rich.But, like many luxuries, as they became more popular and more accessible to the masses, the wealthy began pivoting – a textbook example of behaviour known as "counter signalling", Rudolfo says."The same way that logo bags are considered gauche or quiet luxury is more aspirational, bare nails are considered the trend now."The examples are almost always white women or celebrities... [and] they'll often conflate class and taste with that bareness."Others point out bare nails often demand their own time-consuming and costly routine."The irony in all this is these natural nails are not natural either," Shapiro says. "They also require a lot of grooming and sometimes pretty premiere services."Few would argue there aren't valid feminist questions for the beauty industry to answer, around unrealistic standards for example, but the largely female-run nail sector also feels empowering for many women."I feel like nail care has very much had a 'for women, by women' sort of ethos around it," Shapiro says. "The first salon opened in New York City was owned by a woman, and she was a remarkably independent one... a lot of the first entrepreneurs offering product lines, opening salons were women."Hampton admits she's saddened by the way trends have been – and continue to be - weaponised."We're taking the fun out of nails... Anyone should be able to wear what they like - nail polish or bare nails," she says. "Why is there an argument? Why is there beef?"Scanlon too is a little baffled."For me, it's like, just stop judging ourselves and everybody else," she says. "Some people like to have the nails done, some people don't. "I suppose the question that I was posing was, is it doing anything for you?"The truth of it is: it's not that deep."

schema.headline: Classy or classist? How bare nails became a hot issue
